title: Didactic example — sort algorithms ↔ time complexity
description: A realistic comprehension exercise — match standard sort algorithms to their average-case time complexity. Demonstrates DragMatch as the primary assessment widget for taxonomy-style learning content.

data.markdown:
## Average-case time complexity

We use $O(\cdot)$ to describe how an algorithm's running time scales with input size $n$, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. "Average case" assumes a random permutation of inputs — distinct from worst case (adversarial input) and best case (already-sorted input, etc.).

Match each sort algorithm below to its average-case bound.

sections.title: Match each sort to its average-case complexity

data.prompt: Drag each sort algorithm into the row that gives its AVERAGE-case time complexity.
data.explanation: Bubble and insertion sort both run in O(n²) average — every element compares with most others. Quicksort, merge sort, and heap sort all hit O(n log n) — divide-and-conquer or partial-order data structures. Counting sort sidesteps comparison entirely and runs in O(n + k) where k is the value range — fast for small integer keys but linear in k, not n.
